reference.source: Manson's Tropical Diseases; WHO guidance on lymphatic filariasis
clinicalPearls: A hypersensitivity reaction to lymphatic filarial parasites (Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia species) affecting the lungs
Typically presents with paroxysmal nocturnal cough, wheeze and breathlessness that can mimic asthma
Occurs in residents of, or travellers from, filariasis-endemic areas of South Asia, Southeast Asia, Africa and the Pacific
Marked peripheral blood eosinophilia and a very high serum immunoglobulin E are hallmark laboratory findings
Antifilarial antibody titres are strongly positive, whereas microfilariae are characteristically absent from the peripheral blood because they are trapped and destroyed in the tissues
Chest imaging often shows diffuse reticulonodular or miliary shadowing, predominantly in the mid and lower zones
Diethylcarbamazine is the mainstay of treatment and usually produces rapid clinical improvement
Delayed or inadequate treatment can lead to chronic interstitial lung disease and fibrosis
reference.pathophysiology: Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia is an immunological hyperresponsiveness to lymphatic filarial worms rather than a direct tissue infection by adult worms in the lung. Microfilariae released into the circulation are rapidly cleared from the blood by an exuberant immune response and become trapped in the pulmonary vasculature and interstitium. There they trigger intense eosinophil recruitment and release of eosinophil granule proteins and inflammatory mediators, driven by a strong immunoglobulin E and antifilarial antibody response. This causes bronchospasm, alveolar and interstitial inflammation, and, if untreated, progressive interstitial fibrosis.
additionalDifferentials: Loeffler syndrome from transpulmonary helminth migration (Ascaris, hookworm, Strongyloides)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film demonstrating marked eosinophilia
Serum total immunoglobulin E and antifilarial antibody serology
Chest radiograph and, where needed, high-resolution CT of the chest
Examination for the absence of circulating microfilariae (including night blood films in the filarial context)
Pulmonary function testing showing restrictive or mixed patterns
Exclusion of other causes of pulmonary eosinophilia (sputum for fungi and mycobacteria, stool for helminths)
redFlags: Progressive breathlessness or hypoxaemia despite treatment, suggesting established fibrosis
Failure to respond to antifilarial therapy, prompting review of the diagnosis
Very high eosinophil counts with systemic features raising concern for a hypereosinophilic syndrome
Signs of an alternative serious diagnosis such as tuberculosis or vasculitis
reference.prognosis: With prompt antifilarial treatment most patients recover fully, but diagnostic delay or recurrent untreated episodes can result in chronic interstitial lung disease and irreversible pulmonary fibrosis.
pitfalls: Managing the illness as ordinary asthma and missing the filarial cause
Expecting to find microfilariae in the blood, whose characteristic absence supports the diagnosis
Overlooking a relevant travel or residence history in an endemic region
Attributing the eosinophilia to allergy alone without serological confirmation
Under-treating and allowing progression to fibrosis
management: Give a course of the antifilarial diethylcarbamazine as the mainstay to eliminate the microfilarial trigger
Add bronchodilators and, in severe or slowly responding disease, corticosteroids to control airway and interstitial inflammation
Monitor symptoms, eosinophil count and lung function for relapse, repeating the antifilarial course if symptoms recur
Watch for progression to chronic interstitial lung disease and pulmonary fibrosis when treatment is delayed
Exclude other causes of pulmonary eosinophilia before and during treatment
Advise on vector avoidance and filariasis exposure in endemic areas
